title: Given a Scenario, Troubleshoot Common Personal Computer Security Issues

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: PC security incidents often appear first as symptoms: network failure, strange alerts, altered files, update problems, pop-ups, certificate warnings, redirects, or slow browser performance.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Recognize whether a PC symptom points toward malware, browser compromise, certificate trouble, altered files, or disrupted security services while remembering that each symptom can also have a non-malicious cause.

sections.title: Common Symptoms
paragraphs: Classify the user's strongest clue before selecting a response. Several related symptoms appearing together provide a stronger security signal than one isolated symptom.

sections.title: Unable to Access the Network
paragraphs: A compromised PC may lose network access because malware changes proxy or DNS settings, manipulates the firewall, disables an adapter, or damages network configuration. Ordinary network causes must still be checked.
sections.callout: Networking worked before suspicious software appeared → investigate malicious configuration changes.

sections.title: Desktop Alerts
paragraphs: Unexpected desktop alerts may come from malware, adware, fake antivirus software, or an unwanted application. Do not trust a message merely because it appears on the desktop.
sections.callout: Identify which application created the alert.

sections.title: False Alerts Regarding Antivirus Protection
paragraphs: Scareware may report many infections, claim protection expired, demand payment, or insist on an urgent download.
sections.callout: An unknown security product using fear and demanding action → false antivirus alert.

sections.title: Altered System or Personal Files
paragraphs: Malware may modify, rename, delete, or encrypt files and may also change system configuration without permission.
sections.callout: Files changed without user authorization → possible compromise.

sections.title: Missing, Renamed, or Inaccessible Files

entries.title: Missing or Renamed Files
paragraphs: Unexpected missing or renamed files can result from malware, ransomware, corruption, or user error. Widespread changes combined with other suspicious behavior increase concern.

entries.title: Inability to Access Files
paragraphs: Files that still exist but cannot be opened may be encrypted by ransomware, blocked by changed permissions, corrupted, or affected by other malware.

sections.callout: Missing means the file is not where expected; inaccessible means it exists but cannot be opened.

sections.title: Unwanted Notifications Within the OS
paragraphs: Unexpected operating-system notifications may come from potentially unwanted programs, adware, browser notification permissions, or malicious applications.
bullets: Review installed applications
Inspect browser notification permissions
Check startup items
Identify the notification source
sections.callout: Do not merely dismiss repeated messages; find their source.

sections.title: OS Updates Failures
paragraphs: Malware may disable or interfere with update services to prevent security fixes. Network problems, insufficient storage, corrupt update components, and damaged system files can produce the same symptom.
sections.callout: A sudden update failure is a clue, not automatic proof of malware.

sections.title: Browser-Related Symptoms
paragraphs: The published browser symptoms are random or frequent pop-ups, certificate warnings, redirection, and degraded browser performance. Determine whether the problem is limited to the browser or affects the entire PC.

sections.title: Random and Frequent Pop-Ups
paragraphs: Persistent pop-ups can indicate adware, a malicious extension, browser-notification abuse, or a compromised website.
sections.callout: Pop-ups that do not stop → inspect the browser, extensions, permissions, and adware.

sections.title: Certificate Warnings
paragraphs: A browser certificate warning can result from an expired certificate, hostname mismatch, untrusted certificate authority, incorrect system time, or intercepted connection. Do not blindly bypass it.
sections.callout: The browser cannot verify site trust; also check the system clock.

sections.title: Redirection
paragraphs: Unexpected browser redirection sends the user to a destination they did not select. Possible causes include a malicious extension, adware, DNS manipulation, or a browser hijacker.
sections.callout: The user selects site A but is sent to site B → redirection.

sections.title: Degraded Browser Performance
paragraphs: A slow browser can result from excessive extensions or tabs, malware, adware, corrupt cache, or resource-heavy scripts. If the entire PC is slow, broaden the investigation beyond the browser.
sections.callout: Only the browser is slow → start with the browser; everything is slow → investigate general system performance.

sections.title: Symptom Clustering
paragraphs: One symptom may have an innocent explanation. Pop-ups, redirects, a fake antivirus alert, and degraded browser performance appearing together strongly suggest malicious or unwanted software.
sections.callout: One clue → investigate; several related clues → stronger security signal.

sections.title: PC Security Troubleshooting Flow
bullets: Identify whether the symptom affects networking, alerts, files, updates, or the browser
Review recent applications, extensions, and downloads
Verify antivirus, firewall, and update status
Isolate the system when malware is suspected and follow the Objective 2.6 removal procedure
Remediate the cause and verify normal operation

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Network unavailable after suspicious change → possible malware or network modification
Strange desktop warning → malicious or unwanted software
Fake antivirus demand → scareware
Files modified unexpectedly → possible malware
Files renamed or missing → possible ransomware or malware
Files exist but cannot be opened → encryption, permission, corruption, or malware
Unexpected OS notifications → unwanted program, adware, or malware
OS updates suddenly fail → possible security interference
Repeated pop-ups → adware or browser compromise
Certificate warning → trust, time, or interception issue
Browser goes to the wrong site → redirection or hijacking
Browser alone becomes slow → browser, extension, or malware issue

sections.title: Objective 3.4 Exam Trap
bullets: A real antivirus alert comes from a known installed product; fake antivirus uses fear to demand payment or action.
A pop-up is an extra unwanted message or window; redirection automatically sends the browser elsewhere.
Missing files no longer appear where expected; inaccessible files exist but cannot be opened.
A certificate warning does not automatically mean malware—check validity, hostname, trust chain, and system time.
Browser-only slowness points to browser troubleshooting; whole-system slowness points to broader resource troubleshooting.
Update failure may result from malware, storage, networking, or corruption; treat it as a clue rather than proof.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Lost network after suspicious change → possible compromise
Strange desktop warning → desktop alert
Fake virus notification → scareware
Files changed unexpectedly → malware indicator
Files missing or renamed → possible ransomware or malware
Files locked or inaccessible → possible encryption or permission compromise
Unexpected OS notifications → adware, unwanted program, or malware
Security updates will not run → possible malware interference
Many pop-ups → adware or browser compromise
Invalid certificate warning → certificate, trust, or time issue
Browser goes elsewhere → redirection
Only the browser becomes slow → browser-related performance issue
